title: MANDEL: Jail sentence shock for speeding cop in killing of teen
article: The judge seemed to be leaning his way: York Regional Police Det.-Const. Remo Romano wouldn't be spending time behind bars.

Earlier this year, Romano, 47, was convicted at his third trial of dangerous driving causing the death of 18-year-old Natasha "Carla" Abogado on Feb. 12, 2014. The detective was doing 115 km/h in a 60 km/h zone in his undercover Ford F-150 truck - without emergency lights or siren - to catch up to his surveillance team when he struck and killed the young woman jaywalking across St. Clair Ave. E. from a bus stop to to her home.
Now after a hung jury, an acquittal, a successful Crown appeal and now a conviction, he was finally going to learn his fate.

The Crown was asking for a year in jail. Defence lawyer Bill MacKenzie argued the exemplary officer shouldn't be incarcerated for a tragic accident. As he began reading his reasons for sentence, Ontario Superior Court Justice Brian O'Marra seemed to be siding with Romano.

While Crown attorney Mabel Lai had argued that the officer showed no remorse for what he did, O'Marra disagreed. The judge said Romano expressed remorse both in a pre-sentence report and in open court during sentencing submissions in June.

He also found the dedicated father of five had an otherwise impeccable record as a police officer - he's been on administrative duties since he was charged - and that he'd suffered trauma on the job, including the murder of fellow surveillance team member Rob Plunkett in 2007.

The judge also noted that Romano has been diagnosed with PTSD due to Abogado's death: "The ongoing stressors and triggers ... have created an inability to address recovery and management of the initial trauma."
Has he suffered enough, as his lawyer had argued?

O'Marra then turned to the Abogado family who sat anxiously in the front row of the packed courtroom: Sonia and Guillermo immigrated from the Philippines in 2003 to give their children a better life and their beloved Carla had been the"second parent" to her two younger siblings while her parents worked.

"Carla's death has had a devastating impact on the entire family," the judge said. "They have experienced depression, anger and stress. The ongoing legal proceedings were a constant reminder of the loss of Carla."
That devastating loss must be reflected in his sentence, O'Marra warned. Suddenly it seemed jail time was back on the table.
"A custodial sentence is required," the judge concluded. While the Crown's proposed one-year term was "excessive," O'Marra sentenced Romano to eight months.
Family members began weeping. His colleagues looked at each other in shock.

"I'm just stunned," admitted his lawyer outside court. "It's a significant jail term that he received. We had hoped given the journey of this case - three trials, 4 1/2 years, all the mitigating factors that the judge spoke highly about - there would have been a suspended sentence so the eight-month jail sentence is, quite frankly, shocking and a great disappointment to the family."
It would also mean the end of his career. If sentenced to jail time, MacKenzie added, there's little chance a police officer would be allowed to keep his job.
But for now, Romano would spend just a few hours in custody.

While he was taken to a holding cell, all the other players walked across the courtyard to the Ontario Court of Appeal where lawyer Frank Addario insisted Romano should be granted bail while he appeals his conviction and sentence.

Among his arguments, Addario told Justice David Paciocco that if not freed on bail, Romano would end up serving his entire sentence before his appeal could even be heard. He's not a flight risk, the proposed grounds of appeal aren't weak and he's always shown up for every court date since he was first charged in 2014, the lawyer added.
To the relief of Romano's friends and family, the judge agreed and released him on bail.
And the Abogado family? They left the appeal court in tears as this never-ending nightmare refuses to end.
